Because sometimes people aren't anxious because they're consuming too much bad news. Sometimes they're anxious because the bad news is their reality. If your house is gone because of a flood, if you're breathing smoke from forest fires, if your livelihood has been destroyed, or if you can't afford basic necessities, the problem isn't simply that you're overwhelmed by information. The problem is that you're living through the consequences.

And that's where the conversation starts to feel disconnected. Mindfulness can help you survive a crisis. It cannot solve a crisis. Breathing exercises won't stop forest fires. Curating your news feed won't fix broken policies. Logging off won't rebuild a collapsed house. And telling people to be psychologically resilient shouldn't become a substitute for asking why people are being put in these situations in the first place.

So isn't just about: "How do we protect our mental health while the world is falling apart?" We also need to ask: "Why is the world falling apart in the first place, and who's responsible for fixing it?" Because if we only teach people how to become more resilient, we risk creating a society that's very good at surviving problems that should have been prevented. And that's the part I think is missing. People don't just need coping mechanisms. They need solutions. They need accountability.
